Here's a full engineering estimate for your feeder disk, with all assumptions called out so you can swap in your actual numbers where you have better data.

## 1. Assumptions (please adjust if these don't match your design)

| Parameter | Assumed value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Disk material | Aluminum, ρ = 2700 kg/m³ | |
| Disk geometry | Solid disk (pockets ignored) | Conservative — pockets remove a little material, so this slightly overestimates disk inertia, which offsets other unmodeled effects |
| Ball pocket radius | 65 mm from center | Reasonable fit for a 100mm-radius disk holding 67mm-diameter balls with a rim; adjust to your actual pocket layout |
| Index angle per ball | 60° (1/6 rev) | 6 pockets |
| Target speed | 60 RPM = 2π rad/s = 6.28 rad/s | |
| Accel/decel time to reach speed | 50 ms | Typical for a "snappy" indexing move — adjust if your motion profile is slower/faster |
| Rotation axis | Vertical (disk horizontal, "lazy susan" style) | **This matters a lot** — see note at the end if your disk actually spins in a vertical plane |

## 2. Rotational Inertia

**Disk (solid cylinder about its center):**
- Volume = π·r²·t = π·(0.1)²·(0.01) = 3.14×10⁻⁴ m³
- Mass = 2700 × 3.14×10⁻⁴ ≈ **0.85 kg**
- I_disk = ½·m·r² = 0.5 × 0.85 × 0.1² ≈ **4.24×10⁻³ kg·m²**

**Balls (point mass approx. at pocket radius, worst case = all 6 loaded):**
- I_ball = m·r_p² = 0.06 × 0.065² ≈ 2.54×10⁻⁴ kg·m² each
- I_balls (×6) ≈ **1.52×10⁻³ kg·m²**

**Total system inertia:**
$$J_{total} ≈ 4.24×10^{-3} + 1.52×10^{-3} ≈ 5.8×10^{-3}\ \text{kg·m}^2$$

## 3. Torque for Acceleration

Angular acceleration to reach 60 RPM in 50 ms:
$$\alpha = \frac{\omega}{t} = \frac{6.28}{0.05} ≈ 125.7\ \text{rad/s}^2$$

Torque to accelerate the disk+balls:
$$T_{accel} = J \cdot \alpha = 5.8×10^{-3} × 125.7 ≈ 0.73\ \text{N·m}$$

## 4. Add Margin for Friction, Cogging, and Uncertainty

Bearing drag, ball-in-pocket friction, air drag, and the fact that real load moments (unbalanced ball loading, misaligned pockets, etc.) aren't captured in the ideal model all eat into available torque. A **~1.75–2x margin** on the dynamic torque is standard practice here:

$$T_{design} ≈ 0.73 × 1.75 ≈ 1.3\ \text{N·m}$$

**Recommendation: select a motor rated for at least 2–3 N·m holding/continuous torque** (roughly 2–3x the bare calculated value). This isn't double-counting margin — it's standard practice because stepper torque droops with speed and coil temperature, and gearmotor ratings often quote peak, not sustained, torque.

## 5. Stepper vs. BLDC Gearmotor

| | NEMA 23 Stepper | BLDC Gearmotor |
|---|---|---|
| Typical holding/rated torque | ~0.9–3 N·m depending on frame length/current (many mid-length NEMA23s land around 1.2–2 N·m) | Highly variable — a small BLDC with a 10:1+ gearbox easily clears several N·m continuous |
| Fit for 1.3 N·m requirement | Comfortable fit for many NEMA23 variants | Also comfortable, but likely oversized/underused unless you need high duty cycle |
| Position accuracy for indexing | Excellent — open-loop, repeatable, natural detent torque holds position at rest without active control | Needs an encoder + closed-loop control to index reliably |
| Behavior at 60 RPM | Low speed for a stepper — well within the flat part of the torque-speed curve, minimal torque droop | Non-issue, BLDCs are speed-agnostic within their range |
| Best suited for | Intermittent, precise start-stop indexing motion (matches your described use case) | Continuous/high-duty-cycle rotation, or very high-cycle-rate feeding |
| Complexity/cost | Lower — simple driver, no feedback loop required | Higher — needs encoder, closed-loop controller |

### Recommendation

Given this is **intermittent indexing** (accelerate, stop precisely at each pocket, hold) rather than continuous rotation, a **NEMA 23 stepper motor** is the better fit. Your calculated torque requirement (~1.3 N·m design torque) sits comfortably within the holding-torque range of common NEMA23 motors, the open-loop repeatability suits pocket-to-pocket indexing well, and 60 RPM is a low enough speed that you won't run into significant torque droop on the speed-torque curve. Look for a motor rated ≥2 N·m holding torque to keep good margin, and consider microstepping + a simple S-curve or trapezoidal motion profile (rather than sharp trapezoids) to reduce resonance/vibration at each index.

Switch to a BLDC gearmotor only if you expect this to evolve into high-cycle-rate or continuous-spin operation (e.g., feeding balls much faster than indexed steps, or running for extended periods where stepper heating becomes a concern).

### One important caveat
If your disk actually rotates in a **vertical plane** (axis horizontal) rather than flat like a lazy susan, gravity will impose an additional torque as unbalanced ball loads swing through different angular positions — this can dominate over the inertial torque calculated above and would need to be added explicitly. Let me know the orientation if that's the case and I can redo the holding-torque analysis with the gravitational moment included.

```vb
'==============================================================================
' Macro:      FeederDisk_CreateBase
' Purpose:    Creates the base geometry for the rotary escapement feeder disk:
'               1. New Part document
'               2. Sketch a 200mm diameter circle on the Top Plane
'               3. Extrude (Boss) the circle to 10mm thickness
'               4. Sketch a 20mm diameter circle centered on the same origin
'               5. Cut-Extrude Through All to create the center motor shaft bore
'
' Notes:
'   - All dimensions are entered in METERS because the SolidWorks API always
'     works in base SI units regardless of the document's display units.
'     (200mm = 0.2m, 10mm = 0.01m, 20mm = 0.02m, radius = diameter / 2)
'   - Tested against SolidWorks API conventions for 2018-2024; adjust the
'     template path below to match a valid part template on your system.
'==============================================================================

Option Explicit

Sub main()

    Dim swApp           As SldWorks.SldWorks
    Dim swModel         As SldWorks.ModelDoc2
    Dim swModelDocExt   As SldWorks.ModelDocExtension
    Dim swSketchMgr     As SldWorks.SketchManager
    Dim swFeatMgr       As SldWorks.FeatureManager
    Dim swFeature       As SldWorks.Feature
    Dim swSketch        As SldWorks.Sketch
    Dim boolStatus      As Boolean
    Dim longStatus      As Long
    Dim longWarnings    As Long

    ' ---- Dimension constants (converted to meters for the API) ----
    Const DISK_DIAMETER_M  As Double = 0.2      ' 200 mm disk diameter
    Const DISK_THICKNESS_M As Double = 0.01     ' 10 mm disk thickness
    Const BORE_DIAMETER_M  As Double = 0.02     ' 20 mm center bore diameter

    Dim diskRadius As Double
    Dim boreRadius As Double
    diskRadius = DISK_DIAMETER_M / 2#
    boreRadius = BORE_DIAMETER_M / 2#

    ' ---- Path to a valid Part template on this machine ----
    ' Update this path if your SolidWorks installation uses a different
    ' template location (Tools > Options > File Locations > Document Templates).
    Dim partTemplatePath As String
    partTemplatePath = "C:\ProgramData\SolidWorks\SOLIDWORKS 2023\templates\Part.prtdot"

    ' Connect to the running instance of SolidWorks
    Set swApp = Application.SldWorks

    If swApp Is Nothing Then
        MsgBox "SolidWorks is not running. Please start SolidWorks and try again.", vbExclamation
        Exit Sub
    End If

    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    ' 1. Create a new Part document
    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    Set swModel = swApp.NewDocument(partTemplatePath, 0, 0, 0)

    If swModel Is Nothing Then
        MsgBox "Failed to create new part. Check that the template path is valid:" & vbCrLf & _
               partTemplatePath, vbCritical
        Exit Sub
    End If

    Set swModelDocExt = swModel.Extension
    Set swSketchMgr = swModel.SketchManager
    Set swFeatMgr = swModel.FeatureManager

    ' Set document units to millimeters (MKS / mm, gram, second) for display purposes
    ' (does not affect API calls below, which remain in meters)
    swModel.SetUnits swLengthUnit_e.swMM, swMassPropertyUnit_e.swMASS_PROPERTY_KILOGRAMS, _
                      swMassPropertyUnit_e.swMASS_PROPERTY_MILLIMETERS, False, False, False

    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    ' 2. Select the Top Plane and open a new sketch
    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    boolStatus = swModelDocExt.SelectByID2("Top Plane", "PLANE", 0, 0, 0, False, 0, Nothing, 0)
    If Not boolStatus Then
        MsgBox "Could not select Top Plane.", vbCritical
        Exit Sub
    End If

    swSketchMgr.InsertSketch True   ' True = attempt to align/exit gracefully if needed

    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    ' 3. Draw the 200mm diameter circle centered at the sketch origin
    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    ' CreateCircle takes center point (x,y,z) and a point on the circle (x,y,z),
    ' all in meters, in the sketch's coordinate system.
    Dim skCircle As SldWorks.SketchSegment
    Set skCircle = swSketchMgr.CreateCircle(0, 0, 0, diskRadius, 0, 0)

    ' Exit the sketch (this becomes Sketch1 - the disk profile)
    swSketchMgr.InsertSketch True

    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    ' 4. Extrude the disk profile to 10mm thickness
    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    ' Select the sketch we just created before extruding
    boolStatus = swModelDocExt.SelectByID2("Sketch1", "SKETCH", 0, 0, 0, False, 0, Nothing, 0)
    If Not boolStatus Then
        MsgBox "Could not select Sketch1 for extrusion.", vbCritical
        Exit Sub
    End If

    ' FeatureExtrusion3 parameters (key ones used here):
    '   Sd (bool)        = True  -> feature is a Boss/Base extrusion
    '   Flip (bool)      = False -> do not flip direction
    '   Dir (bool)       = False -> single direction (not "both directions")
    '   T1 (long)        = 0     -> swEndConditions_e.swEndCondBlind (blind extrude)
    '   T2 (long)        = 0     -> end condition for direction 2 (unused here)
    '   D1 (double)      = DISK_THICKNESS_M -> depth of extrude in direction 1 (meters)
    '   D2 (double)      = 0     -> depth in direction 2 (unused)
    Set swFeature = swFeatMgr.FeatureExtrusion3( _
        True, False, False, _
        swEndConditions_e.swEndCondBlind, swEndConditions_e.swEndCondBlind, _
        DISK_THICKNESS_M, 0, _
        False, False, False, False, _
        0, 0, _
        False, False, False, False, True, _
        True, True, _
        0, 0, False)

    If swFeature Is Nothing Then
        MsgBox "Boss extrusion failed.", vbCritical
        Exit Sub
    End If

    ' Rename the feature for clarity
    swFeature.Name = "Disk_Base_Extrude"

    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    ' 5. Sketch the 20mm center bore on the same Top Plane
    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    boolStatus = swModelDocExt.SelectByID2("Top Plane", "PLANE", 0, 0, 0, False, 0, Nothing, 0)
    If Not boolStatus Then
        MsgBox "Could not select Top Plane for bore sketch.", vbCritical
        Exit Sub
    End If

    swSketchMgr.InsertSketch True

    Dim skBore As SldWorks.SketchSegment
    Set skBore = swSketchMgr.CreateCircle(0, 0, 0, boreRadius, 0, 0)

    swSketchMgr.InsertSketch True   ' Exit sketch -> becomes Sketch2

    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    ' 6. Cut-Extrude the center bore Through All (both directions safe
    '    in case sketch plane orientation differs from expected)
    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    boolStatus = swModelDocExt.SelectByID2("Sketch2", "SKETCH", 0, 0, 0, False, 0, Nothing, 0)
    If Not boolStatus Then
        MsgBox "Could not select Sketch2 for cut feature.", vbCritical
        Exit Sub
    End If

    ' FeatureCut4 parameters (key ones used here):
    '   Sd (bool)      = True  -> single-ended cut
    '   Flip (bool)    = False -> do not flip cut direction
    '   Dir (bool)     = False -> single direction
    '   T1 (long)      = swEndCondThroughAll -> cut through entire disk thickness
    '   D1 (double)    = 0     -> not used with Through All end condition
    Set swFeature = swFeatMgr.FeatureCut4( _
        True, False, False, _
        swEndConditions_e.swEndCondThroughAll, swEndConditions_e.swEndCondThroughAll, _
        0, 0, _
        False, False, False, False, _
        0, 0, _
        False, False, False, False, False, _
        True, True, True, _
        False, 0, 0, False, False)

    If swFeature Is Nothing Then
        MsgBox "Cut-extrude for center bore failed.", vbCritical
        Exit Sub
    End If

    swFeature.Name = "Center_Bore_Cut"

    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    ' 7. Zoom to fit and finish
    '--------------------------------------------------------------------
    swModel.ViewZoomtofit2

    MsgBox "Feeder disk base geometry created successfully:" & vbCrLf & _
           "- Diameter: 200 mm" & vbCrLf & _
           "- Thickness: 10 mm" & vbCrLf & _
           "- Center bore: 20 mm", vbInformation

End Sub
```

To use it: open SolidWorks, go to Tools > Macro > New, paste this in, save, and run it (or press F5 in the VBA editor).

## Wear Analysis: Bare 6061-T6 Aluminum vs. Delrin-Lined Pockets

### 1. The Core Problem: Tennis Ball Felt as an Abrasive

Tennis ball felt isn't just "fuzzy" — it's a nylon/wool blend fiber matrix embedded with fine abrasive particulate (manufacturing residue, court debris, and clay/hard-court grit picked up during use). Combined with the fact that your pockets will see **thousands of load/unload cycles** with repeated sliding contact as balls seat and eject, this is a classic case of **three-body abrasive wear** — the felt fibers act as a carrier that drags embedded grit across the pocket surface repeatedly.

This matters because it changes which failure mode you're actually designing against: it's not primarily *adhesive* wear (metal-on-metal galling) — it's **abrasive scoring and surface fatigue** from a felt-borne grit slurry, which favors different material choices than you'd pick for a simple friction problem.

### 2. Friction Coefficient Comparison

| Interface | Approx. Coefficient of Friction (kinetic) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Tennis felt vs. bare 6061-T6 Aluminum | **0.4 – 0.6** | Aluminum's relatively soft, oxide-forming surface has high adhesion/friction against textile fibers; oxide layer (Al₂O₃) is hard but brittle and gets abraded away, exposing fresh soft aluminum underneath repeatedly |
| Tennis felt vs. Delrin (Acetal, POM) | **0.15 – 0.35** | Delrin is renowned in engineering for having one of the lowest friction coefficients of any unlubricated engineering plastic against textiles and elastomers — it's the reason Delrin is a default choice for gears, bushings, and conveyance components |

**This is roughly a 2x reduction in kinetic friction** by switching the pocket contact surface to Delrin — which directly reduces both the sliding force needed to seat/eject balls and the energy dissipated as heat and material loss at the interface.

### 3. Wear Mechanism Comparison

**Bare 6061-T6 Aluminum:**
- 6061-T6 is a good structural aluminum but has **poor intrinsic abrasion resistance** — Brinell hardness ~95 HB, notably softer than most engineering plastics people assume "outperform" metals on.
- The natural aluminum oxide layer (~60-70 HRC equivalent, very hard) is only a few microns thick. Under repeated abrasive felt contact, this oxide layer is **continuously breached and re-formed**, exposing soft base aluminum to further wear each cycle.
- Result: **visible pocket wall polishing, then scoring/pitting** over time, with wear debris (aluminum particulate) potentially contaminating the mechanism and altering pocket geometry — which for a precision indexing feeder means drift in ball-seating repeatability over the product's life.

**Delrin-Lined Pockets:**
- Delrin (POM-C or POM-H) has excellent **abrasion resistance relative to its hardness** because of its low surface energy and crystalline structure — it resists fiber "grabbing" and doesn't gall.
- Critically, Delrin is **self-lubricating**, meaning friction (and thus heat generation and wear rate) stays low and consistent even in dry, unlubricated, repeated-cycle service — exactly your use case.
- It also has enough resilience to slightly cushion ball impact/seating, which bare aluminum does not, reducing surface fatigue at the pocket walls from repeated impact loading (each ball dropping in has a nontrivial impact velocity at 60 RPM indexing).
- Long-term wear shows as **gradual, predictable, cosmetic surface dulling** rather than material loss/pitting, and Delrin liners are simple, low-cost replaceable wear parts if needed.

### 4. Practical/Engineering Considerations

| Factor | Bare Aluminum | Delrin Lining |
|---|---|---|
| Manufacturing complexity | None (as-machined) | Requires pocket inserts, bonded liner, or overmold — added step |
| Cost | Lowest | Low-moderate (Delrin stock is inexpensive; added labor for liner fitting) |
| Weight impact | None | Negligible (Delrin inserts are thin, low density ~1.41 g/cm³) |
| Long-term dimensional stability | Wears/enlarges pockets over time → looser ball seating → indexing repeatability drift | Maintains pocket geometry much longer |
| Serviceability | Requires full disk replacement/re-machining if worn | Liners can be designed as replaceable wear parts |
| Noise/impact | Harder impact, more mechanical noise on ball seating | Slightly dampened, quieter operation |

### 5. Recommendation

**Add Delrin liners or inserts to the ball pockets.** Given that this is a mechanism expected to run continuous, repeated indexing cycles with direct abrasive textile contact, bare 6061-T6 aluminum is a genuinely poor match for the *actual* wear mode at play — abrasive, fiber-driven surface degradation, not just simple sliding friction. The friction coefficient alone (roughly halved with Delrin) already justifies the change from a motor-loading standpoint, but the more important factor is that Delrin's wear characteristics directly counter the specific abrasive mechanism tennis felt presents, while aluminum's protective oxide layer offers no lasting defense against it.

**Practical implementation path:** rather than coating (which is harder to apply durably and consistently to a curved pocket geometry), I'd recommend **machining the pockets slightly oversized and press-fitting or bonding thin (1.5–3mm) Delrin pocket inserts** — this is simpler to manufacture reliably than a true coating process (like anodizing + PTFE impregnation, which would be the metal-only alternative), costs very little in material, and gives you a defined, replaceable wear item rather than wear directly on your structural disk.

If you'd like, I can help size the insert geometry (wall thickness, retention method — press fit vs. adhesive vs. mechanical clip) or extend the SolidWorks macro to model the pockets as a two-part assembly (aluminum disk + Delrin insert) rather than a single-body cut.

## ISO Fit Recommendation for the 20mm Center Bore

### First, a quick terminology check

You referenced "shaft-basis... H7/h6" — worth flagging that **H7/h6 is actually hole-basis notation** (the capital "H" denotes the hole is the fixed reference with zero fundamental deviation; lowercase letters denote the shaft grade). True shaft-basis notation would look like "K7/h6" (shaft fixed, hole varies).

That said, this distinction matters less than it seems here: **industry practice defaults to hole-basis (H-basis) almost universally**, even though physically your shaft is the "given" (off-the-shelf motor shaft, typically ground to h6). This is because standard reamers, boring tools, and gauges are economically sized to produce clean H-grade holes — it's cheaper to hold tight tolerance on the bore you're machining than to try to match an arbitrary shaft tolerance with custom tooling. So I'd recommend sticking with hole-basis (H7 bore) as your reference system, even though the shaft is technically the constraint.

### Selecting the fit type

The critical engineering question isn't just "does the shaft fit in the bore" — it's **what's actually transmitting the ~1.3 N·m design torque** we calculated earlier for the indexing motion. A few options:

| Fit class | Example | Behavior | Suitability here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clearance | H7/h6, H7/g6 | Free assembly/disassembly by hand, but relies entirely on a key/pin/set-screw for torque — pure friction at this clearance won't reliably hold under start-stop torque spikes | Workable only if paired with a robust key or set screw |
| **Transition** | **H7/k6, H7/n6** | Near-zero clearance to slight interference; self-centers with minimal wobble, still hand/light-press assembleable | **Best fit for this application** |
| Interference | H7/p6 | Requires press or thermal assembly; effectively permanent | Overkill/impractical for a serviceable feeder disk |

### Recommendation: **Ø20 H7/k6**

- **Bore:** Ø20 H7 → **+0.021 / 0 mm**
- **Mating shaft:** Ø20 k6 → **+0.015 / +0.002 mm**

This gives a tolerance stack ranging from about **0.002mm interference to 0.019mm clearance** — tight enough to eliminate wobble that would otherwise translate into pocket-positioning error during indexing, but still assembleable without a press or heat gun.

**Important:** this transition fit alone should not be your sole torque-transmission method. Friction/interference at this fit class is not a reliable substitute for a positive mechanical driver, especially given the acceleration torque spikes calculated earlier. Pair it with **either**:
- A key + keyway (best for repeated high-cycle service, prevents any slip over the product's life), or
- A set screw on a shaft flat (simpler to machine, adequate if torque margin is generous and cyclic loading is moderate)

If you truly want to lock the shaft's tolerance as the fixed reference (genuine shaft-basis system, useful if you're sourcing multiple motor variants with a guaranteed h6 shaft spec), the equivalent callout is **K7 (bore) / h6 (shaft)**. I'd recommend confirming the exact K7 deviation values against an ISO 286-2 table before committing them to your drawing — those numbers are worth double-checking against the standard rather than relying on memory, unlike the H7/h6/k6 values above which are well-established.

---

## GD&T Concentricity Callout

### Why "Concentricity" (as a literal GD&T symbol) is usually the wrong choice

Under **ASME Y14.5-2018**, the true Concentricity symbol (⊚) is explicitly discouraged in modern practice — it requires establishing median points of diametrically opposed surface elements, which is essentially impossible to verify practically on a CMM and is rarely used in current industry drawings. **ISO 1101** still permits it, but even there, most practicing engineers substitute a more inspectable control.

Since this is a **rotating component** where your actual functional concern is dynamic wobble/imbalance during 60 RPM indexing (not just static bore-to-OD coincidence), the more appropriate and practically verifiable controls are:

### Recommended callout: Position tolerance (primary) or Total Runout (if dynamic wobble is the main concern)

**Setup:**
- **Datum A = Outer Diameter (OD)** — this is the feature your disk will most likely be chucked/located on during both machining and inspection, and functionally represents the rotational reference.

**Option 1 — Position (preferred for manufacturability/CMM inspection):**
```
⌖ | ⌀0.05 | Ⓜ | A
```
Reads as: the bore's axis must fall within a Ø0.05mm cylindrical tolerance zone relative to Datum A, evaluated at Maximum Material Condition. This is standard modern practice, CMM-friendly, and directly controls what actually matters — the bore staying centered relative to the disk's rotational reference.

**Option 2 — Total Runout (if you specifically care about dynamic wobble/balance, e.g. for vibration control during indexing):**
```
⌰ | 0.05 | A
```
This is often the more *functionally* honest callout for a spinning part, since it simultaneously captures coaxiality, circularity, and perpendicularity errors in a single dial-indicator-measurable spec — directly reflecting how the part will behave once it's spinning at 60 RPM.

**If your company standard specifically requires ISO 1101 concentricity** despite the inspection caveats above, the equivalent callout would be:
```
⊚ | ⌀0.03 | A
```

### Practical tolerance value
Given this is an indexing feeder (not a precision optical or bearing application), **0.03–0.05mm** is a reasonable, achievable tolerance band — tight enough to prevent pocket-position drift accumulating across the 6 pockets, without demanding unnecessarily expensive machining/inspection precision.
